fields.Front: Define throughput, and distinguish instantaneous from average throughput.
fields.Back: The rate (bits per unit time) at which bits are delivered from sender to receiver. Instantaneous: rate at a given point in time. Average: rate over a longer period (F bits in T seconds gives F/T).

fields.Front: Throughput for a server-to-client path with link rates Rs and Rc?
fields.Back: min(Rs, Rc): the rate of the bottleneck link. If Rs < Rc throughput is Rs; if Rs > Rc it is Rc.

fields.Text: End-to-end throughput over links Rs and Rc is {{c1::min(Rs, Rc)}}, the rate of the {{c2::bottleneck link}}; for N links in series it is {{c3::min(R1, ..., RN)}}.
The {{c1::bottleneck link}} is the link on the end-to-end path that constrains (limits) the end-to-end throughput.

fields.Front: Numeric: F = 32 million bits, Rs = 2 Mbps, Rc = 1 Mbps. Throughput and transfer time?
fields.Back: Throughput = min(2, 1) = 1 Mbps; T = 32 x 10^6 / 10^6 = 32 s.

fields.Front: Numeric: server access link 10 Mbps, client access link 4 Mbps, uncongested core, 40 Mbit file. Throughput and time?
fields.Back: Throughput = min(10, 4) = 4 Mbps; T = 40 x 10^6 / 4 x 10^6 = 10 s.

fields.Text: 10 connections fairly share a backbone link R; server links Rs, client links Rc. Per-connection throughput = {{c1::min(Rc, Rs, R/10)}}.

fields.Front: Numeric (slide): Rs = 2 bps, Rc = 3 bps, R = 6 bps shared by 10 connections. Per-connection throughput?
fields.Back: min(3, 2, 6/10) = 0.6 bps; the shared backbone link is the bottleneck.

fields.Front: In practice, which link is usually the bottleneck for an Internet connection?
fields.Back: The access links (Rc or Rs), because the Internet core is over-provisioned with high-speed links.
